prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy rules, which underpin the New Keynesian framework for analysing monetary policy.

statement.case_for: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the organising structure of modern monetary-policy analysis and central-bank practice. Calvo's time-dependent pricing device gave the framework a tractable microfoundation. Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule tied it to how policy is actually conducted and evaluated. Woodford's synthesis turned it into a welfare-based theory of optimal policy. The three contributions are distinct but fit together, and the conceptual and practical influence is very large. The work is four decades old and has been through the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. The 2022 prize on banking and financial crises covers a different mechanism, so the overlap is small. Having heard the colleagues' arguments, I keep this as my first choice, but I treat B036 as a close alternative. The case for B036 rests on strong attribution among Autor, Dorn and Hanson and on more than a decade of replication.
statement.case_against: Credit is spread across at least eight serious contributors. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets did much of the Phillips-curve and estimated-DSGE work that made the framework operational. Any three-name cut will be contested, and the Committee may find it hard to defend. The standard model's performance after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation is debated, and heterogeneous-agent extensions are challenging parts of its representative-agent core. Earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims, Bernanke) cover adjacent ground. I also work in macroeconomic theory, so my sense of what is central here may be biased in either direction.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B018 first with the same trio. He sees the framework as the working core of monetary-policy analysis and credits Calvo with staggered pricing, Taylor with the rule and Woodford with the synthesis. He also flags the attribution problem and criticism after 2008 and 2021-23.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the division of credit. I would qualify the criticism point. The 2021-23 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent literature test and extend the framework more than they displace it, since the nominal-rigidity mechanism and the policy-rule logic remain in use. The attribution cost is real, though, and I do not think it can be removed by choosing a different three.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B018 fourth and proposes Calvo, Woodford and Galí. He sees credit as highly dispersed and the empirical record as tested by the crisis and the inflation. His first choice is the misallocation work (B010).
responses.response: Galí is the strongest substitute for Taylor, given the Phillips-curve and policy-analysis work with Gertler and Clarida. I still prefer Taylor, because the rule and the staggered-contracts model are what linked the theory to how policy is conducted and judged. Taylor's contributions also predate much of the later synthesis. On B010, I accept that misallocation changed development accounting. But measured dispersion can reflect markups, adjustment costs and measurement error, and the attribution is incomplete without Rogerson. Those two points keep it below B018 for me.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B036 first. He argues that Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the cleanest attribution for the China-shock work, that Katz's task and skill-premium work overlaps with earlier recognition and another list entry, and that the effects are still debated.
responses.response: This moved me. My opening B036 trio of Autor, Katz and Hanson combined two strands, which is the harder attribution. If the Committee chooses B036, the empirical trade-shock core with Autor, Dorn and Hanson is better supported and has over a decade of replication. I still rank it below B018. The long-run persistence of the effects and the identification choices are contested, and the work overlaps with the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize. I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B047 first as a unified political-economics programme. He notes that the causal identification of constitutional effects in cross-country data is contested and that the 2024 institutions prize may weigh against a related award.
responses.response: I agree that the Persson-Tabellini-Besley programme is coherent and mature, and I ranked it second. I would qualify the 2024 overlap concern. The overlap is thematic, since the formal theory of electoral rules and state capacity is a distinct contribution. Your point about identification is the more serious one, and it is why I do not place it first. It stays my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Taylor or Galí should be the third name, and whether the Committee would accept a trio that omits Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.
How far the 2008 crisis and 2021-23 inflation experience and heterogeneous-agent alternatives reduce the Committee's confidence in the framework as a settled discovery.
Whether B036, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, deserves priority given its stronger opening support and cleaner attribution.
I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified the credit attributions.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names in the preferred configuration is apparent from the supplied profile. The disclosed ties are co-authorship with committee colleagues Timo Boppart and John Hassler, and my own research in macroeconomic theory, which is adjacent to B018 and could bias my judgment. The supplied profile shows no connection to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford.
